sections.title: What are Large Language Models?
sections.body: Large Language Models, or LLMs, are advanced computer systems that understand and generate human language. They are built using a type of artificial intelligence called neural networks, which learn from vast amounts of text data. This training helps them predict what words come next in a sentence.

sections.title: How LLMs Process Text
sections.body: LLMs break down text into smaller pieces called tokens, which can be words, subwords, or even characters. These tokens are transformed into numerical representations, known as embeddings, that capture the meaning and relationships between words. This process allows LLMs to understand context and generate relevant responses.

sections.title: The Importance of Prompts
sections.body: Prompts are the questions or instructions we give to LLMs to guide their responses. Even small changes in a prompt can lead to very different outputs, making prompt design crucial for getting accurate answers. By carefully crafting prompts, we can influence the style and content of the LLM's responses.

sections.title: Enhancing LLM Performance
sections.body: Techniques like prompt engineering and Chain-of-Thought prompting help improve the performance of LLMs. Prompt engineering involves creating structured prompts that lead to better answers, while Chain-of-Thought prompting encourages the model to show its reasoning step-by-step. These methods are especially useful in educational settings where clarity and accuracy are essential.

sections.title: Challenges and Solutions
sections.body: Despite their capabilities, LLMs can produce unreliable outputs, known as hallucinations, especially if prompts are vague or poorly structured. To address this, new tools are being developed that automatically refine prompts, making it easier for users to get reliable and accurate responses from LLMs.

turns.question: How does tokenization influence the embeddings in LLMs?
turns.answer: Tokenization influences embeddings because embeddings are created for tokens, not directly for whole sentences or words.  Step 1: Tokenization  Before an LLM can process text, it breaks the input into tokens.  For example:  "unbelievable"  might become:  ["un", "believ", "able"]  or  ["unbelievable"]  depending on the tokenizer.  Similarly:  "I love learning AI"  might become:  ["I", " love", " learning", " AI"]  Each token is then mapped to a unique ID.  Step 2: Embedding Lookup  Every token ID corresponds to a learned embedding vector.  For example:  Token	ID	Embedding "I"	42	[0.12, -0.31, ...] "love"	105	[0.78, 0.
